note: The permission expression ((mp)) written after the map class mc in the classpermissionset is parsed: the inner list (mp) becomes a sub-expression and is appended to the perms expression as a CIL_LIST item. The attacker-controlled nested list enters the perms data structure here.
The generated perms expression, including the nested CIL_LIST item, is stored as the class-perms perm_strs for the (mc ((mp))) entry of the classpermissionset.

During name resolution the nested list is recursed into and re-appended into the resolved perms list as a CIL_LIST item, so the list structure survives resolution instead of being flattened or rejected.
The class mc resolves to a map class; cp->perms now holds [CIL_LIST: [CIL_DATUM: mp]] -- a nested list containing the resolved map-class permission datum.
The resolved classperms entry (mc ((mp))) is appended to the classpermission cp's classperms list, so the poisoned entry reaches the verification phase.
Pre-verify walks the AST; for CIL_CLASSPERMISSION cp the classperms list (containing the (mc ((mp))) entry) is handed to the class-perms verifier.
Iterating the classperms list: the entry (mc ((mp))) is a CIL_CLASSPERMS item whose data is a struct cil_classperms.
mc is a map class (CIL_MAP_CLASS), so the flawed per-permission handling branch for map classes is taken.

The perms item is the CIL_LIST (nested list); the condition treats it as a permission-datum path. The faulty assumption that every non-operator item is a permission datum is what mishandles lists in permission expressions.
i->data, which is a struct cil_list *, is cast to struct cil_perm *cmp and cmp->classperms is dereferenced at a bogus offset, reading out of bounds and crashing during class permission verification.
